prompt.context: Your client is Slick Hick, a large agricultural equipment manufacturer. Its primary product line, farming tractors, is losing money.
prompt.question: What questions would you ask of your client to help them solve their profitability problem?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors?
clarifying_info.a: There are two direct competitors.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current market share breakdown?
clarifying_info.a: Client has 40% of the market, Competitor 1 has 30%, Competitor 2 has 15%, and the remaining 15% belongs to many small manufacturers.

clarifying_info.q: What was market share five years ago?
clarifying_info.a: Five years ago the client had 60%, Competitor 1 had 15%, and Competitor 2 had 10%. The client has lost significant share to its two main competitors.

clarifying_info.q: Are all three competitors selling to the same customers?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, all three competitors sell to the same customers.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client's pricing compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The client's product is priced higher than others. This has always been the case.

clarifying_info.q: Why does the client command a premium price?
clarifying_info.a: The client has a strong reputation and image of quality. The market has historically been willing to pay a premium because it implied a longer-lasting, more reliable product — critical for farmers who cannot afford equipment breakdowns.

clarifying_info.q: Are the products functionally the same?
clarifying_info.a: All products share the same basic features, but tractors are not commodity items and a few differences do exist.

clarifying_info.q: Have revenues changed?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues are down.

clarifying_info.q: Has sales quantity changed?
clarifying_info.a: Quantity is down.

clarifying_info.q: Has price changed?
clarifying_info.a: Prices are up.

clarifying_info.q: Have costs changed?
clarifying_info.a: Costs are up.

clarifying_info.q: Have fixed costs changed?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs are unchanged.

clarifying_info.q: Have variable costs changed?
clarifying_info.a: Variable costs have increased tremendously. The client does not know why.

clarifying_info.q: Is the client a manufacturer or assembler?
clarifying_info.a: Primarily assembly.

clarifying_info.q: Have finished part prices changed?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, finished part prices have gone up.

clarifying_info.q: Have raw material prices for suppliers changed?
clarifying_info.a: Not to the client's knowledge.

clarifying_info.q: Have supplier labor costs or supplier composition changed?
clarifying_info.a: No change in supplier labor costs and no change in suppliers.

clarifying_info.q: Why have finished part prices gone up?
clarifying_info.a: The prices have increased as a result of product improvement efforts. The client has tightened tolerances and improved the durability of component parts.

clarifying_info.q: Why did the client make product improvements?
clarifying_info.a: The client strives to sell the world's best tractors.

clarifying_info.q: Are customers willing to pay for the product improvements?
clarifying_info.a: The client assumed yes, but customers do not appear to place a high value on the improvements.

framework: Profitability = Revenue - Costs; decompose as P*Q - (FC + VC*Q)
Revenue side: examine price and quantity trends separately
Cost side: split fixed vs. variable costs; drill into VC buckets (materials, labor, parts)
Competitive context: benchmark market share trends, pricing, and product features vs. the two main competitors
Customer willingness to pay: assess whether customers value and recognize product improvements
Root cause linkage: connect cost drivers to pricing decisions and resulting volume impact

questions.prompt: Diagnose the revenue decline — what has happened to price and volume?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates identify that price is up but volume is down, suggesting price elasticity is at play. The revenue decline is driven by quantity loss (market share erosion from 60% to 40%) rather than price cuts.

questions.prompt: Diagnose the cost increase — what type of costs have risen and why?
questions.guidance: Fixed costs are flat; variable costs have increased significantly. The VC increase traces to higher finished-part prices, which in turn stem from the client's own product improvement efforts (tighter tolerances, more durable components) — not from supplier inflation or labor changes.

questions.prompt: Connect the root cause: why is the client losing money?
questions.guidance: The client raised part quality (raising VC), then raised prices to recover those costs, but customers do not sufficiently value the improvements. This created a price-value mismatch that drove volume loss and net profitability decline. The client assumed customer willingness to pay without validating it.

brainstorming.prompt: What should Slick Hick do to restore profitability?

categories.name: Cost repositioning
ideas: Scale back product improvement program to reduce VC
Negotiate with suppliers to find cost-efficient ways to achieve quality goals
Evaluate whether all tolerance upgrades are necessary or if some can be reversed without degrading perceived quality

categories.name: Revenue / pricing
ideas: Re-evaluate pricing strategy to close the gap with competitors where improvements are not valued
Segment customers: identify farmers who do value reliability and price-sensitive farmers separately
Explore premium sub-brand for reliability-focused customers vs. a value line for price-sensitive customers

categories.name: Marketing and customer education
ideas: Improve marketing to communicate the value of product improvements to customers
Provide ROI data (e.g., fewer breakdowns, longer lifespan) to justify premium pricing
Use case studies or testimonials from farmers who have benefited from improved reliability

categories.name: Competitive benchmarking
ideas: Assess competitors' R&D investment and product improvement trajectories before scaling back
Understand whether competitors are closing the quality gap, which would erode the premium rationale
Monitor whether Competitor 1 and 2 share gains are driven by price, product, or distribution

categories.name: Process improvement
ideas: Implement a cost/benefit analysis step in the product improvement process before committing to upgrades
Create customer feedback loops to validate willingness to pay before investing in VC-increasing changes
Pilot improvements with a customer segment before rolling out broadly

recommendation: Slick Hick should immediately implement a cost/benefit analysis gate in its product improvement process to ensure future VC increases are only approved when customer willingness to pay is validated
In the near term, evaluate which recent component upgrades can be rolled back without materially affecting perceived quality, to reduce VC and allow more competitive pricing
Review and strengthen marketing to ensure customers understand and recognize the value of quality improvements that are retained
risks: Scaling back product improvements could accelerate quality parity with competitors, eroding the premium brand position that is the client's core differentiator
If competitors continue to invest in R&D while Slick Hick pulls back, the client risks losing its quality leadership permanently
Price reductions to recover volume may compress margins further if VC is not simultaneously reduced
recommendation.risks_note: Evaluate competitor R&D positions before making irreversible product decisions
next_steps: Conduct customer research to quantify willingness to pay for specific improvements
Audit all recent component upgrades and rank by cost impact vs. customer-perceived value
Benchmark competitor R&D spend and product roadmap
Design a stage-gate process for future product improvements requiring customer validation before full rollout
